notes.meaning: God rebukes Jerusalem for forgetting how He cared for her when she was young and weak. Instead of being thankful, she grew furious against His ways and indulged in shameful idolatry. Because of this, the Lord brings the consequences of her choices right back down on her own head.

People who love clever sayings will use a common proverb to describe Jerusalem: like mother, like daughter. The city acted so much like the corrupt pagan nations that lived in Canaan before her that she took after their worst habits.

Jerusalem belonged to an ungodly family line in terms of her behavior. Her ancient predecessors, the Hittites and Amorites, rejected God and even offered their own children as sacrifices to idols. Jerusalem followed the exact same brutal, unfaithful path.

The Lord compares Jerusalem to two neighboring cities, calling them her sisters. Her northern sister was the larger kingdom of Samaria, and her southern sister was ancient Sodom, along with their surrounding villages. Both places had already faced ruin for their wicked behavior.

Jerusalem did not merely copy the bad examples of her neighbors. She considered their evil too small a thing and raced ahead of them in corrupt living. In a very short time, she became far worse than either sister ever was.

The Lord swears an oath by His own life to drive this shocking truth home. Even Sodom, known everywhere as the ultimate symbol of evil, had never sunk as low in wicked deeds as Jerusalem and her towns had done.

God explains the root sins that started Sodom on the road to ruin. The people of Sodom were arrogant, stuffed with food, and totally relaxed in their comfortable lives. Because they were selfish, they never lifted a hand to help the poor or needy.

Sodom's pride grew into open defiance, leading to terrible and detestable deeds right before God's eyes. When the Lord saw how corrupt they had become, He wiped them completely off the earth. Great comfort without love for others quickly leads to destruction.

The northern kingdom of Samaria had not done even half the wrong that Jerusalem had done. Jerusalem committed so many disgusting acts of idol worship that she actually made her wicked sisters look good by comparison.

Jerusalem used to look down on her sisters and judge them as terrible sinners. Now she has to bear her own heavy shame, because her vile deeds made those other cities seem almost justified—meaning declared less guilty—when compared to her.

God says He will restore the fortunes of Sodom and Samaria, and He will restore Jerusalem right in the middle of them. Jerusalem is placed on the very same footing as these ruined places, tearing away every last bit of her pride.

When Jerusalem is restored alongside these places, she will feel thoroughly ashamed of her past. Her own downfall and suffering gave a kind of sad comfort to Sodom and Samaria, who saw that God's chosen city was punished just like them.

God promises that Sodom and Samaria, along with their villages, will return to their former state, and Jerusalem will return with them. God makes it clear that Jerusalem will not be elevated above the others in pride, but will share in this mercy together.
Back when Jerusalem was prosperous and proud, she refused to even speak the name of Sodom. She thought she was far too holy and special to ever end up like that destroyed city.

Jerusalem acted proud until her own evil was uncovered and her enemies invaded her land. Now she suffers the very same mocking and contempt from neighbors like Syria and Philistia that she once directed at others.

The Lord announces that Jerusalem must carry the full penalty for her unfaithfulness and detestable sins. The suffering she faces is not God being unfair, but the exact harvest of her own evil choices.

God declares that He will pay Jerusalem back according to what she did. She took a sacred oath to belong to the Lord at Mount Sinai, but then threw that covenant away like trash, freeing God to punish her as a traitor.

Right when hope seems gone, God announces that He will remember the covenant He made with Israel in her youth. Out of His own pure mercy, He will set up an everlasting covenant with her that can never be broken.

When other nations come into this family of faith, Jerusalem will receive them as daughters and remember her old ways with deep shame. These foreign nations will be joined to God not through the old law of Moses, but through God's free promise of grace.

The Lord confirms that He will personally establish this unbreakable covenant with His people. Through this act of rescue, they will finally know who He really is: a God of holy justice, perfect truth, and unfailing love.

God will make atonement—meaning He will wipe out and cover all the wrongs Jerusalem ever did. When she sees such incredible forgiveness, she will be completely silenced from boasting or making excuses, resting only in humble gratitude.
